title: Ὁ ἰὸς Ἀλεξάνδρου
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Diomedes and Odysseus kill two sons of Merops, a seer who had forbidden them the war, and Zeus, watching from Ida, keeps the fighting even. Diomedes wounds Agastrophus, and Hector charges with the Trojan ranks. Diomedes’ spear strikes Hector’s helmet, the helmet Apollo gave him, and Hector is stunned; he recovers while Diomedes goes to fetch his spear, and drives off. Diomedes jeers at him, and while he strips Agastrophus, Alexander, hidden behind the tomb of Ilus, shoots him through the foot. Alexander leaps out in triumph, and Diomedes answers with contempt; Odysseus stands in front of him while he draws the arrow out, and Diomedes drives off to the ships. Odysseus, left alone, talks himself into standing his ground as the Trojans close round him like hunters round a boar. He wounds Deiopites and kills Thoon, Ennomus and Chersidamas, and stabs Charops, whose brother Socus comes to defend him and challenges Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἑλέτην δίφρόν τε καὶ ἀνέρε δήμου ἀρίστω
υἷε δύω Μέροπος Περκωσίου, ὃς περὶ πάντων
ᾔδεε μαντοσύνας, οὐδὲ οὓς παῖδας ἔασκε
στείχειν ἐς πόλεμον φθισήνορα·
sentences.tr:
enth’ heletēn diphron te kai anere dēmou aristō
huie dyō Meropos Perkōsiou, hos peri pantōn
ēidee mantosynas, oude hous paidas easke
steichein es polemon phthisēnora·
sentences.l:
There the two took a chariot and two men, the best of the people,
two sons of Merops the Percosian, who beyond all others
knew seercraft, and nor his own sons did he keep allowing
to go to man-wasting war;
sentences.i: There the two took a chariot and killed two men, the best of the people, two sons of Merops of Percote, who knew the arts of prophecy beyond all others, and would not allow his own sons to go to the war that wastes men;
sentences.n: The ones who act are Diomedes and Odysseus, the dual subject carried over from the end of the last part; they are not named until 333 and 335. ἑλέτην is the dual aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’: with a chariot it means ‘capture’, with men ‘kill’, so the English says both. ἀνέρε … ἀρίστω are duals, ‘two men, best’, with δήμου ‘of the people’. Περκωσίου is the adjective of Percote (named at 2.835). Lines 329–331 are 2.831–833 word for word, where the pair are named Adrastus and Amphius. ἔασκε is iterative, ‘kept allowing’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δέ οἱ οὔ τι
πειθέσθην·
sentences.tr:
tō de hoi ou ti
peithesthēn·
sentences.l:
but those two to him not at all
obeyed;
sentences.i: but the two of them did not obey him at all;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 331. τὼ is the dual pronoun ‘those two’, the sons; οἱ is ‘to him’; οὔ τι ‘not at all’. πειθέσθην is the dual imperfect of πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes the dative. The same words stand at 2.833–834. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 332.

sentences.t: κῆρες γὰρ ἄγον μέλανος θανάτοιο.
sentences.tr: kēres gar agon melanos thanatoio.
sentences.l: for the death-spirits of black death were bringing them on.
sentences.i: for the spirits of black death were bringing them on.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 332. κῆρες is the plural of κήρ ‘death-spirit’, the powers that carry men off to death, not to be confused with the neuter κῆρ ‘heart’ (as in 400); μέλανος θανάτοιο is ‘of black death’. ἄγον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω, ‘were bringing’, and the sons, whom the verb brings on, are not named again. The line is 2.834.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν Τυδεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Διομήδης
θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς κεκαδὼν κλυτὰ τεύχε’ ἀπηύρα·
sentences.tr:
tous men Tydeïdēs dourikleitos Diomēdēs
thymou kai psychēs kekadōn klyta teuche’ apēura·
sentences.l:
These, for his part, Tydeus’-son, famed-for-the-spear Diomedes,
having deprived of heart and of life, the famous armour took away;
sentences.i: These two Diomedes, son of Tydeus, famed for his spear, deprived of heart and life, and took their famous armour;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν is ‘these, for his part’, the two sons of Merops, answered by Ἱππόδαμον δέ in 335. Τυδεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Tydeus’, and δουρικλειτὸς Διομήδης ‘Diomedes, famed for his spear’ is a stock epithet. κεκαδών is a rare reduplicated aorist participle, ‘having deprived (of)’, with the genitive of what is taken: θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς, ‘of heart and of life’, as in the Odyssey’s θυμοῦ καὶ ψυχῆς κεκαδήσει (21.153). κλυτά is ‘famous’, and ἀπηύρα the aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’.

sentences.t: Ἱππόδαμον δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ Ὑπείροχον ἐξενάριξεν.
sentences.tr: Hippodamon d’ Odyseus kai Hypeirochon exenarixen.
sentences.l: but Hippodamus Odysseus despoiled, and Hypirochus.
sentences.i: while Odysseus killed Hippodamus and Hypirochus and stripped them of their armour.
sentences.n: δ’ answers the μέν of 333, ‘these … but these’. ἐξενάριξεν is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of armour’ (from ἐνάρα ‘spoils’), and one verb serves both objects, Ἱππόδαμον and Ὑπείροχον; Ὀδυσεύς stands between the two objects in the Greek, and the literal layer moves ‘and Hypirochus’ to the end so that it reads. The Greek says nothing more about the two men.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά σφιν κατὰ ἶσα μάχην ἐτάνυσσε Κρονίων
ἐξ Ἴδης καθορῶν·
sentences.tr:
entha sphin kata isa machēn etanysse Kroniōn
ex Idēs kathorōn·
sentences.l:
There for them evenly the fighting stretched the son of Cronus,
from Ida looking down;
sentences.i: There, looking down from Ida, the son of Cronus stretched the fighting out evenly between them;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, in this scene. σφιν is ‘for them’, the two sides, and κατὰ ἶσα ‘evenly, in equal measure’; μάχην ἐτάνυσσε is ‘stretched the fighting’, a rope drawn out equally between two teams, so that neither side gains. Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus, who watches ἐξ Ἴδης καθορῶν ‘from Ida looking down’ (Zeus took his seat on the peaks of Ida at 11.183); καθορῶν is the contracted present participle of καθοράω.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἀλλήλους ἐνάριζον.
sentences.tr: toi d’ allēlous enarizon.
sentences.l: and they were despoiling one another.
sentences.i: and they went on killing and stripping one another.
sentences.n: τοί, the article used as a pronoun, is the two armies. ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω ‘strip a man of his armour’ (from ἐνάρα ‘spoils’), which for fighters who kill and strip each other takes in both acts. ἀλλήλους is ‘one another’. The line sums up the even fighting that Zeus is watching.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι Τυδέος υἱὸς Ἀγάστροφον οὔτασε δουρὶ
Παιονίδην ἥρωα κατ’ ἰσχίον·
sentences.tr:
ētoi Tydeos huios Agastrophon outase douri
Paionidēn hērōa kat’ ischion·
sentences.l:
For his part, Tydeus’ son wounded Agastrophus with a spear,
Paion’s-son, the hero, in the hip;
sentences.i: For his part, the son of Tydeus stabbed the hero Agastrophus, son of Paion, in the hip with his spear;
sentences.n: ἤτοι (printed as one word) with the name sets Diomedes against Hector, who comes in at 343. Τυδέος υἱός ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. Παιονίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Paion’; the father’s name Παίων is to be kept apart from the god Παιήων ‘Paieon’. ἥρωα is ‘hero’. οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound, stab’, and κατ’ ἰσχίον ‘in the hip’. The unit stops at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ἐγγὺς ἔσαν προφυγεῖν, ἀάσατο δὲ μέγα θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
ou de hoi hippoi
engys esan prophygein, aasato de mega thymōi.
sentences.l:
but not for him were the horses
near, to flee away on, and he was greatly bewildered in his heart.
sentences.i: but his horses were not near enough for him to escape on, and he was greatly bewildered in his heart.
sentences.n: οὐ δέ (printed as two words) is ‘and not’; οἱ is ‘for him’. ἐγγὺς ἔσαν προφυγεῖν is ‘were near, to flee away’: ἔσαν is the epic ‘were’ (= ἦσαν) and προφυγεῖν the aorist infinitive of προφεύγω; the horses are what he would have fled on. ἀάσατο is the aorist middle of ἀάω ‘bewilder’, from ἄτη ‘bewilderment’, here a lapse of judgement that left him on foot, as the next lines show; the clause is the one at 9.537. μέγα is adverbial, ‘greatly’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν γὰρ θεράπων ἀπάνευθ’ ἔχεν, αὐτὰρ ὃ πεζὸς
θῦνε διὰ προμάχων, εἷος φίλον ὤλεσε θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
tous men gar therapōn apaneuth’ echen, autar ho pezos
thyne dia promachōn, heios philon ōlese thymon.
sentences.l:
For them, on the one hand, the attendant kept apart, but he on foot
rushed through the front-fighters, until he lost his dear life;
sentences.i: for his attendant was keeping the horses apart, while he himself rushed on foot through the foremost fighters until he lost his life;
sentences.n: γάρ explains why the horses were out of reach. τοὺς μέν is ‘those, for their part’, the horses of 339, which the attendant, θεράπων, was keeping ἀπάνευθε ‘apart’ (ἔχεν is the unaugmented imperfect). αὐτὰρ ὃ πεζός is ‘but he on foot’. θῦνε, unaugmented imperfect of θύνω, is ‘rushed’, and διὰ προμάχων ‘through the front-fighters’. εἷος is ‘until’ (= ἕως), and φίλον … θυμόν, ‘dear life’, is the life that leaves a dying man.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὀξὺ νόησε κατὰ στίχας, ὦρτο δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς
κεκλήγων·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ oxy noēse kata stichas, ōrto d’ ep’ autous
keklēgōn·
sentences.l:
And Hector sharply noticed through the ranks, and rushed upon them
shrieking;
sentences.i: Hector was quick to notice them along the ranks and rushed upon them with a shrill cry;
sentences.n: δ’ marks the new subject, Hector. ὀξὺ νόησε is ‘sharply noticed’ (ὀξύ is an adverb here, as in the same words at 5.680 and 8.91), and κατὰ στίχας ‘through the ranks’; νόησε has no object in the Greek, and ‘them’ is supplied from ἐπ’ αὐτούς. ὦρτο is the aorist of ὄρνυμι in the middle voice, ‘rushed’, and κεκλήγων the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek’. Compare 5.590, where the same two verbs stand with ἐνόησε. The unit stops at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἅμα δὲ Τρώων εἵποντο φάλαγγες.
sentences.tr: hama de Trōōn heiponto phalanges.
sentences.l: and together followed the battle-lines of the Trojans.
sentences.i: and the battle-lines of the Trojans followed along with him.
sentences.n: ἅμα is ‘together, at the same time’, with no noun to say who goes with whom: the lines go with Hector. εἵποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, and Τρώων φάλαγγες is ‘the battle-lines of the Trojans’, φάλαγξ being a line of fighting men.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ῥίγησε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης,
αἶψα δ’ Ὀδυσσῆα προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.tr:
ton de idōn rhigēse boēn agathos Diomēdēs,
aipsa d’ Odyssēa prosephōneen engys eonta·
sentences.l:
And him, having seen, shuddered Diomedes, good at the war-cry,
and at once spoke to Odysseus, who was near:
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, shuddered when he saw him, and at once spoke to Odysseus, who was near him:
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Hector. ῥίγησε is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, said of Diomedes, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is his stock epithet. The first line is 5.596 (there with a raised dot), the second Odyssey 22.163: προσεφώνεεν is the epic uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’, and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα ‘who was near’ agrees with Ὀδυσσῆα. The unit stops at the raised dot, and a speech follows.

sentences.t: νῶϊν δὴ τόδε πῆμα κυλίνδεται ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: nōïn dē tode pēma kylindetai obrimos Hektōr·
sentences.l: “To us two indeed this woe is rolling, mighty Hector;
sentences.i: “This woe is rolling down on the two of us: mighty Hector;
sentences.n: Diomedes warns Odysseus. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘to us two’. τόδε πῆμα ‘this woe’ is the subject of κυλίνδεται ‘is rolling on’, as a boulder rolls; ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ ‘mighty Hector’ then names the woe, and ὄβριμος is a stock epithet. δή is ‘indeed’. The Greek carries no quotation marks. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ στέωμεν καὶ ἀλεξώμεσθα μένοντες.
sentences.tr: all’ age dē steōmen kai alexōmestha menontes.
sentences.l: But come now, let us take our stand and defend ourselves, staying firm.”
sentences.i: But come, let us make a stand and defend ourselves by holding our ground.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. στέωμεν is the epic aorist subjunctive of ἵστημι (Attic στῶμεν), ‘let us take our stand’, and ἀλεξώμεσθα the subjunctive of ἀλέξομαι ‘ward off, defend oneself’; both are exhortations. μένοντες is the participle of μένω, ‘staying, standing fast’, and gives the manner of the defence: they hold their ground.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
καὶ βάλεν, οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε τιτυσκόμενος κεφαλῆφιν,
ἄκρην κὰκ κόρυθα·
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai ampepalōn proïei dolichoskion enchos
kai balen, oud’ aphamarte tityskomenos kephalēphin,
akrēn kak korytha·
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit him, and did not miss as he aimed at the head, on the top of the helmet;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί (the edition prints a comma after ῥα) is ‘he spoke, and’; ἦ is the old ‘he said’. ἀμπεπαλών ‘brandishing’ and δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος ‘long-shadowed spear’ are the words of 3.355 and 5.280. βάλεν is ‘hit’; the man hit, Hector, is not named. οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε is ‘and did not miss’, and τιτυσκόμενος ‘aiming’. κεφαλῆφιν has the ending -φιν, here ‘at the head’. ἄκρην κὰκ κόρυθα is ‘on the top of the helmet’, κὰκ being κατά before κ-.

sentences.t:
πλάγχθη δ’ ἀπὸ χαλκόφι χαλκός,
οὐδ’ ἵκετο χρόα καλόν·
sentences.tr:
planchthē d’ apo chalkophi chalkos,
oud’ hiketo chroa kalon·
sentences.l:
and the bronze was driven off course from the bronze,
nor did it reach the fair skin;
sentences.i: and the bronze glanced off the bronze, and did not reach his fair skin;
sentences.n: πλάγχθη is the aorist passive of πλάζω ‘drive off course’, said of the spear-point, and ἀπὸ χαλκόφι χαλκός ‘the bronze from the bronze’ sets point against helmet; χαλκόφι has the old ending -φι, ‘from the bronze’. οὐδ’ ἵκετο is ‘nor did it reach’ (ἵκετο is unaugmented), and χρόα καλόν ‘fair skin’, with χρόα the accusative of χρώς. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἐρύκακε γὰρ τρυφάλεια
τρίπτυχος αὐλῶπις, τήν οἱ πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.tr:
erykake gar tryphaleia
triptychos aulōpis, tēn hoi pore Phoibos Apollōn.
sentences.l:
for the helm held it back,
three-folded, tubed, which to him gave Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.i: for the helmet kept it out, the three-layered, tubed one, which Phoebus Apollo had given him.
sentences.n: ἐρύκακε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and τρυφάλεια is ‘helm’, as in 5.182 (there with αὐλῶπις, the same epithet, ‘tubed’, from αὐλός ‘tube’; its sense is not known). τρίπτυχος is ‘three-folded’, from τρι- and πτύξ ‘fold, layer’. τήν οἱ πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is ‘which Phoebus Apollo gave him’, οἱ being Hector; the same words end 1.72, where the god’s gift is the seer’s art.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὦκ’ ἀπέλεθρον ἀνέδραμε, μίκτο δ’ ὁμίλῳ,
στῆ δὲ γνὺξ ἐριπὼν καὶ ἐρείσατο χειρὶ παχείῃ
γαίης·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ ōk’ apelethron anedrame, mikto d’ homilōi,
stē de gnyx eripōn kai ereisato cheiri pacheiēi
gaiēs·
sentences.i: Hector ran quickly back a very great distance and mingled with the throng; he crashed down and came to a stand on his knees, and propped himself on the ground with a stout hand;
sentences.n: ὦκ’ ἀπέλεθρον ἀνέδραμε is ‘quickly ran back an immeasurable (distance)’: ἀπέλεθρον is an adjective used as an adverb of distance, and ἀνέδραμε is the aorist of ἀνατρέχω ‘run back’. μίκτο is the aorist middle of μίγνυμι, unaugmented, ‘mingled’, with the dative ὁμίλῳ ‘throng’. στῆ δὲ γνὺξ ἐριπών, ‘stood on his knees, having crashed down’, and ἐρείσατο χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘propped himself with a stout hand’ are the words of 5.309; γαίης is the genitive after ἐρείδομαι, ‘on the earth’. The unit stops at the raised dot, after γαίης.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δὲ ὄσσε κελαινὴ νὺξ ἐκάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: amphi de osse kelainē nyx ekalypsen.
sentences.l: and around his two eyes dark night covered.
sentences.i: and dark night covered his eyes all round.
sentences.n: ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’, with ἐκάλυψεν ‘covered’; ὄσσε is the dual ‘two eyes’, and κελαινὴ νὺξ ‘dark night’ is the blackout that comes over him, as at 5.310. The spear has not pierced him (352), so the faint is the effect of the blow on his head.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα δὲ Τυδεΐδης μετὰ δούρατος ᾤχετ’ ἐρωὴν
τῆλε διὰ προμάχων, ὅθι οἱ καταείσατο γαίης
τόφρ’ Ἕκτωρ ἔμπνυτο,
sentences.tr:
ophra de Tydeïdēs meta douratos ōichet’ erōēn
tēle dia promachōn, hothi hoi kataeisato gaiēs
tophr’ Hektōr empnyto,
sentences.l:
And while Tydeus’-son went after the rush of the spear
far through the front-fighters, to where for him it had sped down into the earth,
meanwhile Hector recovered his breath,
sentences.i: And while the son of Tydeus went after the flight of his spear, far through the foremost fighters, to where it had come down in the ground, Hector meanwhile drew breath again,
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα is ‘while … meanwhile’. μετὰ δούρατος ᾤχετ’ ἐρωήν is ‘went after the spear’s rush’: ἐρωή ‘rush’, here the spear’s flight, with μετά + accusative ‘after’ and ᾤχετο ‘went’ (οἴχομαι). ὅθι οἱ καταείσατο γαίης is ‘to where, for him, it had sped down into the earth’; καταείσατο is taken as the aorist middle of ἵεμαι ‘speed’ with κατά ‘down’ (as εἴσατο at 4.138), and γαίης as the genitive of the place. ἔμπνυτο is an old aorist of ἐμπνύω ‘recover breath’, unaugmented. The unit stops at the comma in the middle of 359.

sentences.t:
καὶ ἂψ ἐς δίφρον ὀρούσας
ἐξέλασ’ ἐς πληθύν,
sentences.tr:
kai aps es diphron orousas
exelas’ es plēthyn,
sentences.l:
and back into the chariot having sprung,
drove out into the crowd,
sentences.i: and sprang back into his chariot and drove off into the crowd,
sentences.n: ὀρούσας is the aorist participle of ὀρούω ‘spring’, ἂψ ‘back’, and δίφρον ‘chariot’. ἐξέλασε is the aorist of ἐξελαύνω ‘drive out’; the Greek gives it no object, since the chariot is what he drives. ἐς πληθύν is ‘into the crowd’, πληθύς being the mass of his own men. The unit stops at the comma in the middle of 360.

sentences.t: καὶ ἀλεύατο κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr: kai aleuato kēra melainan.
sentences.l: and avoided the black death-fate.
sentences.i: and avoided the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: ἀλεύατο is the aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’, unaugmented, with the words of 3.360, where Alexander ‘avoided the black death-fate’ in just this way. κῆρα μέλαιναν is ‘the black death-fate’: κήρ, accusative κῆρα, is the death-spirit, not the neuter κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t: δουρὶ δ’ ἐπαΐσσων προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: douri d’ epaïssōn prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And with his spear rushing at him addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Charging at him with his spear, strong Diomedes spoke:
sentences.n: Diomedes speaks as Hector escapes. δουρί is the dative ‘with his spear’, and ἐπαΐσσων the participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’, and κρατερός ‘strong’ is the stock epithet. The line is 10.369 word for word. A speech follows.

sentences.t: ἐξ αὖ νῦν ἔφυγες θάνατον κύον·
sentences.tr: ex au nyn ephyges thanaton kyon·
sentences.l: “Out again now you fled death, dog;
sentences.i: “Once more you have escaped death, you dog;
sentences.n: ἐξ … ἔφυγες is a verb split in two, ‘fled out of’, with θάνατον ‘death’ as its object; αὖ is ‘again’ and νῦν ‘now’. κύον is the vocative of κύων ‘dog’, an insult. The Greek carries no quotation marks. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 362.

sentences.t:
ἦ τέ τοι ἄγχι
ἦλθε κακόν·
sentences.tr:
ē te toi anchi
ēlthe kakon·
sentences.l:
truly, near to you
came evil;
sentences.i: evil came very near to you;
sentences.n: ἦ τέ is a particle pair, ‘truly’; τοι is the dative ‘to you’ (= σοι); ἄγχι ‘near’. ἦλθε κακόν is ‘evil came’, κακόν being the neuter ‘evil thing’, the spear. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 363.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτέ σ’ ἐρύσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
ᾧ μέλλεις εὔχεσθαι ἰὼν ἐς δοῦπον ἀκόντων.
sentences.tr:
nyn aute s’ erysato Phoibos Apollōn
hōi melleis euchesthai iōn es doupon akontōn.
sentences.l:
now again Phoebus Apollo has guarded you,
to whom you are sure to pray, going into the crash of javelins.
sentences.i: now again Phoebus Apollo has protected you, to whom you must pray when you go into the crash of javelins.
sentences.n: αὖτε is ‘again’. ἐρύσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘protect, guard’ (compare 4.186), and Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the god who gave Hector his helmet (353). ᾧ μέλλεις εὔχεσθαι is ‘to whom you are sure to pray’: μέλλω with an infinitive says what is bound to happen, and εὔχομαι with a god in the dative is ‘pray’. ἰὼν ἐς δοῦπον ἀκόντων is ‘going into the crash of javelins’, δοῦπος ‘crash’ and ἄκων ‘javelin’. The tone is scornful.

sentences.t:
ἦ θήν σ’ ἐξανύω γε καὶ ὕστερον ἀντιβολήσας,
εἴ πού τις καὶ ἔμοιγε θεῶν ἐπιτάρροθός ἐστι.
sentences.tr:
ē thēn s’ exanyō ge kai hysteron antibolēsas,
ei pou tis kai emoige theōn epitarrothos esti.
sentences.l:
Surely I shall finish you off, at least, even later, having met you,
if perhaps some one of the gods is a helper to me too.
sentences.i: I shall surely finish you off even later, when I meet you, if perhaps some one of the gods is a helper to me too.
sentences.n: ἦ θήν is ‘surely’. ἐξανύω is a present with the force of a future, ‘I shall finish’; the verb’s usual sense is ‘accomplish, make an end of’, and with σε it means ‘finish you off’. γε stresses σε, ‘you at least’. ἀντιβολήσας is the aorist participle of ἀντιβολέω ‘meet’. εἴ πού τις … ἐπιτάρροθός ἐστι is ‘if some one … is a helper’: που ‘somewhere, perhaps’, ἔμοιγε ‘to me too’, and ἐπιτάρροθος ‘helper’, as in 5.808.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖ τοὺς ἄλλους ἐπιείσομαι, ὅν κε κιχείω.
sentences.tr: nyn au tous allous epieisomai, hon ke kicheiō.
sentences.l: Now in turn the others I shall go against, whomever I may reach.”
sentences.i: Now I shall go after the others, whoever I can reach.”
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ is ‘now in turn’. ἐπιείσομαι is the future of ἐπιέναι ‘go against’, and τοὺς ἄλλους ‘the others’. ὅν κε κιχείω is ‘whomever I may reach’, with κιχείω the epic aorist subjunctive of κιχάνω ‘reach, find’ (as at 1.26); the singular ὅν is ‘whichever one’. The speech ends at the full stop.

sentences.t: ἦ, καὶ Παιονίδην δουρὶ κλυτὸν ἐξενάριζεν.
sentences.tr: ē, kai Paionidēn douri klyton exenarizen.
sentences.l: He spoke, and Paion’s-son, famous with the spear, he was despoiling.
sentences.i: So he said, and was stripping the son of Paion, famous with the spear, of his armour.
sentences.n: ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ again closes a speech and starts the action. Παιονίδην is Agastrophus, wounded in the hip at 338, and δουρὶ κλυτόν ‘famous with the spear’ is the stock epithet, here said of the man he strips. ἐξενάριζεν is the imperfect of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip’; Agastrophus has already lost his life (342), so only the stripping is left, and the imperfect shows it under way, which is what Paris interrupts.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο
Τυδεΐδῃ ἔπι τόξα τιταίνετο ποιμένι λαῶν,
sentences.tr:
autar Alexandros Helenēs posis ēÿkomoio
Tydeïdēi epi toxa titaineto poimeni laōn,
sentences.l:
But Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
at Tydeus’-son was stretching the bow, the shepherd of the people,
sentences.i: But Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen, was drawing his bow at the son of Tydeus, shepherd of the people,
sentences.n: Ἀλέξανδρος is Paris’ other name, and Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο ‘husband of fine-haired Helen’ is a stock phrase for him (as at 3.329). τόξα τιταίνετο is ‘was stretching the bow’: τόξα is a plural for one bow, and τιταίνομαι ‘stretch’. Τυδεΐδῃ ἔπι is ‘at Tydeus’-son’ (ἔπι stands after its noun, so its accent moves back), and ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Diomedes’ title. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t:
στήλῃ κεκλιμένος ἀνδροκμήτῳ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ
Ἴλου Δαρδανίδαο, παλαιοῦ δημογέροντος.
sentences.tr:
stēlēi keklimenos androkmētōi epi tymbōi
Ilou Dardanidao, palaiou dēmogerontos.
sentences.l:
leaning on a pillar wrought by men’s toil, on the tomb
of Ilus, Dardanus’ descendant, the old elder of the people.
sentences.i: leaning against a pillar raised by men on the tomb of Ilus, a descendant of Dardanus, the old elder of the people.
sentences.n: κεκλιμένος is the perfect passive participle of κλίνω, ‘leaning’, with the dative στήλῃ ‘against a pillar’; a στήλη is an upright slab or pillar, here set on a tomb. ἀνδροκμήτῳ, from ἀνήρ ‘man’ and κάμνω ‘toil’, is ‘wrought by men’s toil’. ἐπὶ τύμβῳ is ‘on the tomb’. Ἴλου Δαρδανίδαο is ‘of Ilus, Dardanus’ descendant’ (the same tomb as at 11.166), and δημογέροντος ‘elder of the people’ (compare 3.149).

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν θώρηκα Ἀγαστρόφου ἰφθίμοιο
αἴνυτ’ ἀπὸ στήθεσφι παναίολον ἀσπίδα τ’ ὤμων
καὶ κόρυθα βριαρήν·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ho men thōrēka Agastrophou iphthimoio
ainyt’ apo stēthesphi panaiolon aspida t’ ōmōn
kai korytha briarēn·
sentences.i: He, for his part, was taking the breastplate off mighty Agastrophus’ chest, and the all-glancing shield from his shoulders, and his heavy helmet;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μέν is ‘he, for his part’, Diomedes, against ὃ δέ in 375, Paris. αἴνυτο is the imperfect of αἴνυμαι ‘take’, with θώρηκα ‘breastplate’ as object and ἀπὸ στήθεσφι ‘from the chest’ (the ending -φι). Ἀγαστρόφου ἰφθίμοιο is ‘of mighty Agastrophus’, ἴφθιμος being a stock epithet. παναίολον is ‘all-glancing’, and ὤμων ‘from the shoulders’ is a genitive of separation. βριαρήν ‘weighty’ is from βρίθω ‘be heavy’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ τόξου πῆχυν ἄνελκε
καὶ βάλεν, οὐδ’ ἄρα μιν ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγε χειρός,
ταρσὸν δεξιτεροῖο ποδός·
sentences.tr:
ho de toxou pēchyn anelke
kai balen, oud’ ara min halion belos ekphyge cheiros,
tarson dexiteroio podos·
sentences.i: and he drew the bow back and hit him, and his shaft did not leave his hand in vain: it struck the flat of his right foot;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is Paris. πῆχυν is the accusative of πῆχυς ‘forearm’; ‘the arm of the bow’ is the part he draws back, and what exactly is meant is not agreed. ἄνελκε is the imperfect of ἀνέλκω ‘draw back’. βάλεν is ‘hit’, and οὐδ’ ἄρα μιν ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγε χειρός is ‘nor did the shaft, then, escape him from his hand in vain’ (ἅλιον ‘in vain’, as at 5.18). ταρσὸν δεξιτεροῖο ποδός is ‘the flat of the right foot’, an accusative of the part struck; ταρσός is a flat surface, and its exact place on the foot is not known. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
διὰ δ’ ἀμπερὲς ἰὸς
ἐν γαίῃ κατέπηκτο·
sentences.tr:
dia d’ amperes ios
en gaiēi katepēkto·
sentences.l:
and right through, the arrow
was fixed in the earth;
sentences.i: the arrow went right through and was planted in the ground;
sentences.n: διὰ … ἀμπερές is διαμπερές ‘right through’, split by δέ; ἰός is ‘arrow’, the same missile as the βέλος ‘shaft’ of 376. κατέπηκτο is the pluperfect passive of καταπήγνυμι ‘fix’, ‘was fixed’, as spears ‘are planted’ at 3.135: the arrow passed through the foot and stood in the ground. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 378.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ μάλα ἡδὺ γελάσσας
ἐκ λόχου ἀμπήδησε καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
ho de mala hēdy gelassas
ek lochou ampēdēse kai euchomenos epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
and he, having laughed very sweetly,
out of the ambush leapt up, and, declaring, spoke a word:
sentences.i: and he laughed with great relish and leapt out of his ambush and said, declaring aloud:
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is Paris. μάλα ἡδὺ γελάσσας is ‘having laughed very sweetly’, the adverb ἡδύ as at 2.270, the laugh of triumph. ἐκ λόχου is ‘out of the ambush’, the cover he shot from, and ἀμπήδησε is ἀνεπήδησε, ‘leapt up’. εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘declaring, spoke a word’; here εὔχομαι is a loud declaration of triumph and not a prayer, as at 5.106. A speech follows.

sentences.t: βέβληαι οὐδ’ ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγεν·
sentences.tr: beblēai oud’ halion belos ekphygen·
sentences.l: “You are hit, and the shaft did not escape in vain;
sentences.i: “You are hit, and my shaft did not go forth in vain;
sentences.n: βέβληαι is the perfect passive of βάλλω, ‘you are hit’. οὐδ’ ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγεν is ‘and the shaft did not escape in vain’, ἅλιον ‘in vain’ as in 376, where the same words are said of his hand; ἔκφυγεν is the aorist of ἐκφεύγω. The Greek carries no quotation marks. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 380.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὄφελόν τοι
νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα βαλὼν ἐκ θυμὸν ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ophelon toi
neiaton es keneōna balōn ek thymon helesthai.
sentences.l:
Would that I had, from you,
struck into the lowest flank and taken the life out.
sentences.i: If only I had hit you in the lowest part of the flank and taken your life from you!
sentences.n: ὡς ὄφελον is the wish ‘would that I had’, ὄφελον being the aorist of ὀφείλω with an infinitive. τοι is σοι, ‘from you’. νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα is ‘into the lowest part of the flank’, κενεών being the hollow of the flank (as at 5.284), βαλών ‘having hit’, and ἐκ … ἑλέσθαι (the preverb standing apart from its verb) ‘to take out’, with θυμόν ‘life’.

sentences.t:
οὕτω κεν καὶ Τρῶες ἀνέπνευσαν κακότητος,
οἵ τέ σε πεφρίκασι λέονθ’ ὡς μηκάδες αἶγες.
sentences.tr:
houtō ken kai Trōes anepneusan kakotētos,
hoi te se pephrikasi leonth’ hōs mēkades aiges.
sentences.l:
So the Trojans too would have breathed again from misfortune,
who bristle at you as bleating goats at a lion.”
sentences.i: Then the Trojans too would have drawn breath again, free of their misfortune, the men who bristle with fear at you, as bleating goats do at a lion.”
sentences.n: οὕτω … ἀνέπνευσαν with κεν is a past conditional, ‘so the Trojans too would have breathed again’ (ἀναπνέω, as at 11.327), with κακότητος ‘from misfortune’, a genitive of what they would be rid of. οἵ τε σε πεφρίκασι is ‘who bristle at you’: πεφρίκασι is the perfect of φρίσσω ‘bristle’, the verb of battle-lines ‘bristling’ with spears (4.282, 7.62), here of fear. μηκάδες αἶγες is ‘bleating goats’, and λέονθ’ is ‘a lion’, the thing they dread.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ οὐ ταρβήσας προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ou tarbēsas prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him then, not terrified, addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Then strong Diomedes, unafraid, spoke to him:
sentences.n: Diomedes answers Alexander. The line is 5.286 word for word. οὐ ταρβήσας is ‘not terrified’, the aorist participle of ταρβέω, and προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes spoke’ is the reply-formula. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
τοξότα λωβητὴρ κέρᾳ ἀγλαὲ παρθενοπῖπα
εἰ μὲν δὴ ἀντίβιον σὺν τεύχεσι πειρηθείης,
sentences.tr:
toxota lōbētēr kerāi aglae parthenopipa
ei men dē antibion syn teuchesi peirētheiēs,
sentences.l:
“Archer, outrager, splendid in your horn, gazer at girls,
if indeed you were to make trial in opposition, with armour,
sentences.i: “You archer, you outrager, so splendid in your horn, you gazer at girls, if you were to make trial of me in open fight, in armour,
sentences.n: Four insults open the speech: τοξότα ‘archer’; λωβητήρ ‘outrager’, from λώβη ‘outrage’; κέρᾳ ἀγλαέ ‘splendid in your horn’ (κέρας is ‘horn’, and whether the bow or a lock of hair is meant is disputed); παρθενοπῖπα ‘gazer at girls’, probably from παρθένος ‘girl’ and ὀπιπεύω ‘look at’ (the formation is not certain). εἰ μὲν δή … πειρηθείης is ‘if indeed you were to make trial’; the Greek gives no object. ἀντίβιον is ‘in opposition’, with σὺν τεύχεσι ‘in armour’.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃσι βιὸς καὶ ταρφέες ἰοί·
sentences.tr: ouk an toi chraismēisi bios kai tarphees ioi·
sentences.l: your bow would not avail you, and your thick arrows;
sentences.i: your bow and your many arrows would be no help to you;
sentences.n: The main clause: οὐκ ἄν … χραίσμῃσι is ‘would not avail’ (ἄν with the aorist subjunctive of χραισμέω), with τοι ‘you’. The subject is βιός ‘bow’ (accented to tell it from βίος ‘life’) and ταρφέες ἰοί ‘thick arrows’: ταρφύς means ‘thick, close-set’, and ἰός is ‘arrow’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ μ’ ἐπιγράψας ταρσὸν ποδὸς εὔχεαι αὔτως.
sentences.tr: nyn de m’ epigrapsas tarson podos eucheai autōs.
sentences.l: but now, having grazed me on the flat of the foot, you declare, just so.
sentences.i: but now you have grazed me on the flat of my foot, and you make this declaration for nothing.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ turns from the imagined fair fight to what has happened. ἐπιγράψας is the aorist participle of ἐπιγράφω, ‘scratch, graze’ (as ἐπέγραψε at 4.139), with μέ and the part grazed in the accusative, ταρσὸν ποδός ‘the flat of the foot’ (compare 377). εὔχεαι is the second person of εὔχομαι in the sense ‘declare’, a loud claim, and αὔτως ‘just so, for nothing’: the claim rests on nothing.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἀλέγω, ὡς εἴ με γυνὴ βάλοι ἢ πάϊς ἄφρων·
sentences.tr: ouk alegō, hōs ei me gynē baloi ē païs aphrōn·
sentences.l: I do not heed it, just as if a woman were to hit me, or a senseless child;
sentences.i: I take no more heed of it than if a woman were to hit me, or a senseless child;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἀλέγω is ‘I do not heed’ (ἀλέγω, as at 8.483), and ὡς εἴ … βάλοι is ‘as if … were to hit’ (an optative): with the first clause it says ‘I care no more than I would if …’. γυνὴ ἢ πάϊς ἄφρων is ‘a woman or a senseless child’, ἄφρων ‘senseless’ (without wits). The comparison is meant to insult. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: κωφὸν γὰρ βέλος ἀνδρὸς ἀνάλκιδος οὐτιδανοῖο.
sentences.tr: kōphon gar belos andros analkidos outidanoio.
sentences.l: for blunt is the shaft of a man without might, a worthless one.
sentences.i: for the shaft of a man who has no might, a worthless man, is blunt.
sentences.n: κωφόν, ‘blunt’, is the word for ‘deaf, dull’; said of a missile it means one that falls dull and does nothing. ἀνδρὸς ἀνάλκιδος οὐτιδανοῖο are two genitives, ‘of a man without might, a worthless one’: ἄναλκις ‘without might’ (ἀ- + ἀλκή) and οὐτιδανός ‘worthless’. γάρ gives the reason he does not heed the wound.

sentences.t:
ἦ τ’ ἄλλως ὑπ’ ἐμεῖο, καὶ εἴ κ’ ὀλίγον περ ἐπαύρῃ,
ὀξὺ βέλος πέλεται, καὶ ἀκήριον αἶψα τίθησι.
sentences.tr:
ē t’ allōs hyp’ emeio, kai ei k’ oligon per epaurēi,
oxy belos peletai, kai akērion aipsa tithēsi.
sentences.l:
Truly otherwise, by me, even if it should touch only a little,
the shaft is sharp, and makes a man spiritless at once.
sentences.i: But a shaft from me, even if it only touches a little, is sharp, and at once makes a man lifeless.
sentences.n: ἦ τ’ ἄλλως is ‘truly otherwise’: a shaft is quite different when it comes ὑπ’ ἐμεῖο ‘from me’ (ὑπό with the genitive of the agent). καὶ εἴ κ’ … ἐπαύρῃ is ‘even if it should touch’: ἐπαύρῃ is an aorist subjunctive of ἐπαυρίσκω, which can mean ‘get a share of’ (as at 1.410) and here ‘touch’. ἀκήριον, from ἀ- and κῆρ ‘heart’, is ‘spiritless’; the sense is inferred from the formation, and ‘lifeless’ is its effect here. τίθησι is ‘makes’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ γυναικὸς μέν τ’ ἀμφίδρυφοί εἰσι παρειαί,
παῖδες δ’ ὀρφανικοί·
sentences.tr:
tou de gynaikos men t’ amphidryphoi eisi pareiai,
paides d’ orphanikoi·
sentences.l:
Of him, the wife’s cheeks are torn on both sides,
and the children orphans;
sentences.i: his wife’s cheeks are torn in mourning, and his children are orphans;
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘of him’, the man my shaft hits, with γυναικός ‘wife’ and παρειαί ‘cheeks’. ἀμφίδρυφοι ‘torn on both sides’ is a form of the adjective ἀμφιδρυφής of 2.700, said there of a wife and here of cheeks scratched in mourning. μέν τε … δέ sets the wife against the children, παῖδες ὀρφανικοί ‘children orphaned’ (ὀρφανικός, as at 6.432). The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 394.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ θ’ αἵματι γαῖαν ἐρεύθων
πύθεται, οἰωνοὶ δὲ περὶ πλέες ἠὲ γυναῖκες.
sentences.tr:
ho de th’ haimati gaian ereuthōn
pythetai, oiōnoi de peri plees ēe gynaikes.
sentences.l:
and he, with blood reddening the earth,
rots, and birds are around him, more than women.”
sentences.i: and he rots, reddening the earth with his blood, and it is the birds, more than the women, that gather round him.”
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is the fallen man. ἐρεύθων is the present participle of ἐρεύθω ‘redden’, with αἵματι ‘with blood’ and γαῖαν ‘the earth’. πύθεται is ‘rots’, the verb used of bones in the rain at Odyssey 1.161. οἰωνοί are the birds that feed on him, and περὶ πλέες ἠὲ γυναῖκες is ‘more around him than women’: περί is an adverb, ‘around’, πλέες ‘more’ (= πλείονες), and ἠέ ‘than’. The speech ends with this image.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δουρικλυτὸς ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
ἔστη πρόσθ’·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tou d’ Odyseus douriklytos engythen elthōn
estē prosth’·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Odysseus, famed-for-the-spear, from close by
having come, stood in front of him;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Odysseus, famed for his spear, came up from close by and stood in front of him;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. τοῦ … πρόσθ’ is ‘in front of him’ (πρόσθε ‘before’ with the genitive, τοῦ being Diomedes), and ἐγγύθεν ἐλθών ‘having come from close by’. δουρικλυτός ‘famed for the spear’ is a stock epithet, the one-word form of δουρὶ κλυτός (2.645, 5.72). Odysseus stands there to screen the wounded man. The unit stops at the raised dot, after πρόσθ’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὄπισθε καθεζόμενος βέλος ὠκὺ
ἐκ ποδὸς ἕλκ’, ὀδύνη δὲ διὰ χροὸς ἦλθ’ ἀλεγεινή.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ opisthe kathezomenos belos ōky
ek podos helk’, odynē de dia chroos ēlth’ alegeinē.
sentences.l:
and he, sitting down behind, the swift shaft
out of his foot was drawing, and pain through his skin came, grievous.
sentences.i: and he, sitting down behind him, was drawing the swift shaft out of his foot, and grievous pain went through his body.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Diomedes, ὄπισθε ‘behind’ Odysseus, and καθεζόμενος ‘sitting down’. βέλος ὠκύ is ‘the swift shaft’, ἐκ ποδός ‘out of his foot’, and ἕλκ’ is ἕλκε, the imperfect, ‘was drawing’. ὀδύνη … ἀλεγεινή is ‘grievous pain’, ἀλεγεινός ‘grievous’; διὰ χροός is ‘through the skin’ (χρώς, ‘body’ in the English), and ἦλθ’ ‘came’.

sentences.t:
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀνόρουσε, καὶ ἡνιόχῳ ἐπέτελλε
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐλαυνέμεν·
sentences.tr:
es diphron d’ anorouse, kai hēniochōi epetelle
nēusin epi glaphyrēisin elaunemen·
sentences.l:
and into the chariot he leapt up, and to the charioteer gave instructions
to drive on to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and he leapt up into the chariot and gave the charioteer instructions to drive to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: Diomedes leaves the fight in the words used of Agamemnon at 273–274. ἀνόρουσε is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘leap up’, and δίφρον is ‘chariot’ here. ἡνιόχῳ is the dative of ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’, ἐπέτελλε is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give instructions’, and ἐλαυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ (Attic ἐλαύνειν). ἔπι stands after its noun, so its accent moves back; νηυσὶν … γλαφυρῇσιν is ‘the hollow ships’, with the epic dative ending -ῃσιν. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 400.

sentences.t: ἤχθετο γὰρ κῆρ.
sentences.tr: ēchtheto gar kēr.
sentences.l: for he was distressed in heart.
sentences.i: for he was distressed at heart.
sentences.n: The reason he leaves: his foot. ἤχθετο is the imperfect of ἄχθομαι ‘be distressed, weighed down’, and κῆρ is ‘heart’ in the accusative of respect, ‘distressed in his heart’. γάρ gives the reason for the order just given. The line is 274 word for word.

sentences.t:
οἰώθη δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δουρὶ κλυτός, οὐδέ τις αὐτῷ
Ἀργείων παρέμεινεν, ἐπεὶ φόβος ἔλλαβε πάντας·
sentences.tr:
oiōthē d’ Odyseus douri klytos, oude tis autōi
Argeiōn paremeinen, epei phobos ellabe pantas·
sentences.l:
And Odysseus, famous with the spear, was left alone, nor did any
of the Argives stay by him, since terror seized all;
sentences.i: Odysseus, famous with the spear, was left alone, and none of the Argives stayed by him, since terror had seized them all;
sentences.n: οἰώθη is the aorist passive of οἰόω ‘leave alone’, ‘was left alone’ (from οἶος ‘alone’). δουρὶ κλυτός is ‘famous with the spear’, the same epithet as δουρικλυτός at 396. οὐδέ τις … παρέμεινεν is ‘nor did any … stay by him’, παραμένω ‘stay beside’. ἐπεὶ φόβος ἔλλαβε πάντας is ‘since terror seized all’: φόβος is the fear that sends men running, and ἔλλαβε is ἔλαβε with its λ doubled for the metre. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr: ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: The poet moves into Odysseus’ mind. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed’, εἶπε ‘spoke’, and πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν ‘to his own great-spirited heart’: he addresses his own θυμός, as in a soliloquy, and ὅς is the possessive ‘his own’. The same line stands at Odyssey 5.298, 5.355, 5.407 and 5.464, where Odysseus also speaks to himself in danger. A speech follows.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγὼ τί πάθω;
sentences.tr: ō moi egō ti pathō;
sentences.l: “Ah me, what am I to suffer?
sentences.i: “Ah me, what is to become of me?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι ἐγώ is ‘ah me’, a cry of distress, and τί πάθω; is ‘what am I to suffer?’: πάθω is the aorist subjunctive of πάσχω in a question of deliberation, ‘what am I to suffer / what is to become of me?’ The same words open his speech at Odyssey 5.465. The question is answered by the two evils he sets out next. The Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
μέγα μὲν κακὸν αἴ κε φέβωμαι
πληθὺν ταρβήσας·
sentences.tr:
mega men kakon ai ke phebōmai
plēthyn tarbēsas·
sentences.l:
a great evil it is, if I take flight,
terrified of the crowd;
sentences.i: It is a great evil if I take flight, terrified of the crowd;
sentences.n: No verb ‘is’ is expressed: μέγα μὲν κακόν is ‘a great evil (it is)’. αἴ κε φέβωμαι is ‘if I take flight’ (φέβομαι, with αἴ κε = ‘if’), and πληθὺν ταρβήσας is ‘terrified of the crowd’, ταρβέω with an accusative of what frightens, as at 6.469. μέν looks forward to τὸ δέ in the next line. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ ῥίγιον αἴ κεν ἁλώω
μοῦνος·
sentences.tr:
to de rhigion ai ken halōō
mounos·
sentences.l:
but the more dreadful thing, if I am caught
alone;
sentences.i: but it is more dreadful still if I am caught alone;
sentences.n: τὸ δὲ ῥίγιον is ‘but the more dreadful thing’; ῥίγιον is the comparative of the stem seen in ῥίγιστα at 5.873, ‘the most dreadful things’. αἴ κεν ἁλώω is ‘if I am caught’, the aorist subjunctive of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be taken’, and μοῦνος is ‘alone’ (= μόνος). The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 406.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους Δαναοὺς ἐφόβησε Κρονίων.
sentences.tr: tous d’ allous Danaous ephobēse Kroniōn.
sentences.l: the other Danaans the son of Cronus has put to flight.
sentences.i: The son of Cronus has put the other Danaans to flight.
sentences.n: This gives the reason he is alone. τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους Δαναούς is ‘the other Danaans’, and ἐφόβησε is the aorist of φοβέω ‘put to flight’, standing for a state that goes on, ‘has put to flight’. Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus, who has been giving Hector the upper hand since 11.186–194.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;
sentences.tr: alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thymos;
sentences.l: But why indeed has my dear heart talked these things over with me?
sentences.i: But why has my own heart talked all this over with me?
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ (= ἦ) is ‘but why, indeed?’: the second thoughts begin. διελέξατο is the aorist middle of διαλέγομαι, ‘talked through, talked over’, with ταῦτα ‘these things’ and μοι ‘with me’. φίλος … θυμός is ‘my dear heart’, φίλος being ‘own’. He reproaches himself for the thought of running.

sentences.t: οἶδα γὰρ ὅττι κακοὶ μὲν ἀποίχονται πολέμοιο,
sentences.tr: oida gar hotti kakoi men apoichontai polemoio,
sentences.l: for I know that the base go away from war,
sentences.i: for I know that the base withdraw from the war,
sentences.n: οἶδα γάρ introduces his answer; ὅττι is ‘that’ (= ὅ τι). κακοί are the base men, the cowards (κακός of men in battle, as at 2.365); ἀποίχονται is the present of ἀποίχομαι ‘go away’, and πολέμοιο the genitive of what they leave, ‘from war’. μέν looks forward to the δέ-clause that follows. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀριστεύῃσι μάχῃ ἔνι τὸν δὲ μάλα χρεὼ
ἑστάμεναι κρατερῶς, ἤ τ’ ἔβλητ’ ἤ τ’ ἔβαλ’ ἄλλον.
sentences.tr:
hos de k’ aristeuēisi machēi eni ton de mala chreō
hestamenai kraterōs, ē t’ eblēt’ ē t’ ebal’ allon.
sentences.l:
but whoever is the best in the fighting, him there is great need
to stand strongly, whether he is hit or hits another.”
sentences.i: but the man who proves best in the fighting, that man must stand his ground strongly, whether he is hit or hits another.”
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κ’ ἀριστεύῃσι is ‘but whoever is the best’ (ἀριστεύω ‘be the best’, as at 6.208), and τὸν δὲ μάλα χρεώ is ‘as for him, there is great need’: χρεώ ‘need’ takes the accusative of the person (τόν) and an infinitive, ἑστάμεναι κρατερῶς ‘to stand strongly’. ἤ τ’ ἔβλητ’ ἤ τ’ ἔβαλ’ ἄλλον is ‘either he is hit or he hits another’: ἔβλητο is the aorist passive of βάλλω, and both verbs are general statements. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὃ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
τόφρα δ’ ἐπὶ Τρώων στίχες ἤλυθον ἀσπιστάων,
sentences.tr:
heios ho tauth’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon,
tophra d’ epi Trōōn stiches ēlython aspistaōn,
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,
meanwhile came on the ranks of the shield-bearing Trojans,
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, the ranks of the shield-bearing Trojans came on,
sentences.n: εἷος (= ἕως) ὃ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε … τόφρα δέ is ‘while he was pondering these things … meanwhile’, the formula for a man in two minds (compare 1.193 and 10.507). ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘ponder’, and κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’. ἤλυθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, and ἀσπιστάων ‘shield-bearing’ the genitive plural of ἀσπιστής. Line 412 is 4.221, which ends there with a raised dot; here it ends with a comma.

sentences.t: ἔλσαν δ’ ἐν μέσσοισι, μετὰ σφίσι πῆμα τιθέντες.
sentences.tr: elsan d’ en messoisi, meta sphisi pēma tithentes.
sentences.l: and they hemmed him in, in the midst of them, setting woe among themselves.
sentences.i: and they hemmed him in among them, bringing woe on themselves.
sentences.n: ἔλσαν is the unaugmented aorist of εἴλω ‘hem in’ (as the Achaeans are to be ‘hemmed in’ at 1.409), with ἐν μέσσοισι ‘in the midst’; the object, Odysseus, is not repeated. μετὰ σφίσι πῆμα τιθέντες is ‘setting woe among themselves’: σφίσι is the reflexive dative ‘for themselves’ and πῆμα ‘woe’, so that the poet warns that the Trojans are making trouble for their own men.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε κάπριον ἀμφὶ κύνες θαλεροί τ’ αἰζηοὶ
σεύωνται,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote kaprion amphi kynes thaleroi t’ aizēoi
seuōntai,
sentences.l:
And as when about a boar dogs and flourishing vigorous young men
rush,
sentences.i: And as when dogs and flourishing young men rush around a boar,
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτε is ‘and as when’, with the subjunctive σεύωνται ‘rush’ (σεύομαι ‘rush, hasten’, as at 6.505). κάπριον is ‘a boar’, and ἀμφί ‘around’ it. θαλεροὶ αἰζηοί ‘flourishing vigorous young men’ stands beside κύνες ‘dogs’: the hunters. The unit stops at the comma in the middle of 415.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ τ’ εἶσι βαθείης ἐκ ξυλόχοιο
θήγων λευκὸν ὀδόντα μετὰ γναμπτῇσι γένυσσιν,
sentences.tr:
ho de t’ eisi batheiēs ek xylochoio
thēgōn leukon odonta meta gnamptēisi genyssin,
sentences.l:
and he comes out of the deep lair,
whetting the white tooth between bent jaws,
sentences.i: while he comes out of the deep lair, whetting his white tusk in his curved jaws,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ τε is ‘and he’, the boar. εἶσι is ‘comes’ (a form of εἶμι), βαθείης ἐκ ξυλόχοιο ‘out of the deep lair’ (ξύλοχος, as in Odyssey 19.445, where a boar also comes out of its lair). θήγων is ‘whetting’, λευκὸν ὀδόντα ‘the white tooth’, which in the English is the boar’s tusk, and μετὰ γναμπτῇσι γένυσσιν ‘between bent jaws’: γναμπτός ‘bent’, γένυς ‘jaw’ (dative plural in -ῃσι). The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ τ’ ἀΐσσονται, ὑπαὶ δέ τε κόμπος ὀδόντων
γίγνεται, οἳ δὲ μένουσιν ἄφαρ δεινόν περ ἐόντα,
sentences.tr:
amphi de t’ aïssontai, hypai de te kompos odontōn
gignetai, hoi de menousin aphar deinon per eonta,
sentences.l:
and around they dart, and beneath, a din of teeth
arises, and they await him at once, dread though he is,
sentences.i: They dart around him, and a din of teeth rises from beneath, and they await him at once, dread though he is,
sentences.n: ἀμφί … ἀΐσσονται is ‘dart around’ (ἀΐσσω, as at 3.367), the dogs and young men. ὑπαί is ‘beneath’ and κόμπος ὀδόντων ‘a din of teeth’, the boar’s tusks gnashing (κόμπος ‘din’, as at Odyssey 8.380); γίγνεται is a general present, as in a simile. οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the hunters, and μένουσιν is transitive here, ‘await’, with ἄφαρ ‘at once’ and δεινόν περ ἐόντα ‘dread though he is’.

sentences.t:
ὥς ῥα τότ’ ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα Διῒ φίλον ἐσσεύοντο
Τρῶες·
sentences.tr:
hōs rha tot’ amph’ Odysēa Diï philon esseuonto
Trōes·
sentences.l:
So then around Odysseus, dear to Zeus, rushed
the Trojans;
sentences.i: so then the Trojans rushed around Odysseus, dear to Zeus;
sentences.n: The simile is applied: ὥς ῥα τότε is ‘so then’. ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect of σεύομαι ‘rush’, with the epic doubled σ; it is the verb of the simile’s σεύωνται. Διῒ φίλον ‘dear to Zeus’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet, with the diaeresis printed. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of 420.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ πρῶτον μὲν ἀμύμονα Δηϊοπίτην
οὔτασεν ὦμον ὕπερθεν ἐπάλμενος ὀξέϊ δουρί,
sentences.tr:
ho de prōton men amymona Dēïopitēn
outasen ōmon hyperthen epalmenos oxeï douri,
sentences.l:
and he first the blameless Deiopites
wounded in the shoulder from above, springing upon him with a sharp spear,
sentences.i: and he first stabbed blameless Deiopites in the shoulder from above, springing upon him with a sharp spear,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is Odysseus. πρῶτον μέν … αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα (422) is ‘first … and then’. ἀμύμονα Δηϊοπίτην is ‘blameless Deiopites’, ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ being a stock epithet that is given even to a Trojan. οὔτασεν ‘wounded’, ὦμον ὕπερθεν ‘in the shoulder from above’ (an accusative of the part struck), ἐπάλμενος ‘springing upon’ (the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι), and ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with a sharp spear’. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Θόωνα καὶ Ἔννομον ἐξενάριξε.
sentences.tr: autar epeita Thoōna kai Ennomon exenarixe.
sentences.l: and then Thoon and Ennomus he despoiled.
sentences.i: and then he killed Thoon and Ennomus and stripped them of their armour.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is ‘but then’. ἐξενάριξε is ‘killed and stripped’, one verb for both Θόωνα and Ἔννομον, as at 335. The Greek names the two men and says nothing more of them.

sentences.t:
Χερσιδάμαντα δ’ ἔπειτα καθ’ ἵππων ἀΐξαντα
δουρὶ κατὰ πρότμησιν ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης
νύξεν·
sentences.tr:
Chersidamanta d’ epeita kath’ hippōn aïxanta
douri kata protmēsin hyp’ aspidos omphaloessēs
nyxen·
sentences.i: And as Chersidamas leapt down from his horses, he stabbed him with his spear in the lower belly, under his bossed shield;
sentences.n: Χερσιδάμαντα is the object, held back for νύξεν ‘stabbed’ (the unaugmented aorist of νύσσω) at the end. καθ’ ἵππων ἀΐξαντα is ‘darting down from the horses’ (the horses stand for the chariot). κατὰ πρότμησιν is ‘in the πρότμησις’, a rare word usually taken to mean the lower belly, where the navel-string was cut; that is the usual explanation and is not certain. ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης is ‘beneath the bossed shield’, ὀμφαλόεσσα ‘bossed’. The unit stops at the raised dot, after νύξεν.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ.
sentences.tr: ho d’ en koniēisi pesōn hele gaian agostōi.
sentences.l: and he, in the dust having fallen, took the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.i: and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Chersidamas. ἐν κονίῃσι πεσών is ‘having fallen in the dust’, with the plural κονίῃσι, and ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ is ‘took the earth with the ἀγοστός’: ἀγοστός is a rare word, usually explained as the crook of the arm or the hollow of the hand, and its exact sense is not known. The picture is of a dying man clutching the ground.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἔασ’, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἱππασίδην Χάροπ’ οὔτασε δουρὶ
αὐτοκασίγνητον εὐηφενέος Σώκοιο.
sentences.tr:
tous men eas’, ho d’ ar’ Hippasidēn Charop’ outase douri
autokasignēton euēpheneos Sōkoio.
sentences.l:
These he left, and he wounded Charops, Hippasus’-son, with a spear,
the own brother of wealthy Socus.
sentences.i: He left these, and stabbed Charops, son of Hippasus, with his spear, own brother of wealthy Socus.
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν is ‘these’, the dead, and ἔασ’ is ἔασε ‘left’, as in εἴασαν at 323. ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and he then’, Odysseus. Ἱππασίδην Χάροπα is ‘Charops, Hippasus’-son’ (Ἱππασίδης, a patronymic), and αὐτοκασίγνητον ‘own brother’ (as at 2.706 and 3.238) stands in apposition. εὐηφενέος is ‘wealthy’, built on εὖ and ἄφενος ‘wealth’, an epithet of Socus; he is the man who speaks next.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπαλεξήσων Σῶκος κίεν ἰσόθεος φώς,
στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰὼν καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ epalexēsōn Sōkos kien isotheos phōs,
stē de mal’ engys iōn kai min pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l:
And to defend him Socus went, a man equal to a god,
and he stood very near, going up, and addressed him with a word:
sentences.i: Socus, a man the equal of a god, went to defend him, and went right up and stood close beside him and spoke to him:
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘for him’, Charops. ἐπαλεξήσων is the future participle of ἐπαλέξω ‘ward off for, defend’, and gives the purpose. Σῶκος κίεν ἰσόθεος φώς is ‘Socus went, a man equal to a god’, with the stock phrase ἰσόθεος φώς and κίεν the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰών is ‘stood very near, going up’, and καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘and addressed him with a word’; μιν is Odysseus, and the edition prints no mark at the line end.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ πολύαινε δόλων ἆτ’ ἠδὲ πόνοιο
σήμερον ἢ δοιοῖσιν ἐπεύξεαι Ἱππασίδῃσι
τοιώδ’ ἄνδρε κατακτείνας καὶ τεύχε’ ἀπούρας,
sentences.tr:
ō Odyseu polyaine dolōn at’ ēde ponoio
sēmeron ē doioisin epeuxeai Hippasidēisi
toiōd’ andre katakteinas kai teuche’ apouras,
sentences.l:
“O Odysseus, much-praised, insatiate of tricks and of toil,
today either over two sons of Hippasus you will vaunt,
two such men having killed and their armour having taken away,
sentences.i: “Odysseus, much-praised, never able to get enough of tricks and toil, today you will either cry out in triumph over two sons of Hippasus, having killed two such men and taken their armour,
sentences.n: Socus speaks. ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ πολύαινε is ‘O Odysseus, much-praised’ (πολύαινος, as at 9.673), and δόλων ἆτα ἠδὲ πόνοιο ‘insatiate of tricks and of toil’, ἆτα being an old vocative, ‘never satisfied’. σήμερον ἤ … ἤ is ‘today either … or’. ἐπεύξεαι is the future of ἐπεύχομαι ‘cry out in triumph’, with the dative δοιοῖσιν Ἱππασίδῃσι ‘over two sons of Hippasus’, Charops and Socus himself. τοιώδ’ ἄνδρε is a dual, ‘two such men’; κατακτείνας ‘having killed’; τεύχε’ ἀπούρας ‘having taken away their armour’.

sentences.t: ἤ κεν ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃς.
sentences.tr: ē ken emōi hypo douri typeis apo thymon olessēis.
sentences.l: or under my spear, struck, you will lose your life.”
sentences.i: or, struck by my spear, you will lose your life.”
sentences.n: The second alternative: ἤ κεν … ὀλέσσῃς is ‘or you will lose’ (κε with the aorist subjunctive, a confident future). ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρί is ‘under my spear’, τυπείς ‘struck’ (the aorist passive participle of τύπτω), and ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃς ‘lose your life’, with ἀπό split from its verb and θυμός meaning ‘life’. The speech ends with the part; Odysseus’ answer is in the next.
